messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 78-year-old retired Database Administrator from North America, has been struggling with the aftermath of his life-threatening illness. The trauma he experienced during this period has left deep scars on his psyche and daily life. Even after recovering from the illness, John finds himself feeling constantly on guard, especially within the safety of his own home. This hypervigilance is a stark contrast to his previous sense of security, as the traumatic event has reshaped how he perceives threat. Any slight sound or movement can send him into a state of high alert, heightening his fear and anxiety. John's memories of the illness are vivid and visceral, often triggered by sensory cues such as particular smells that remind him of the hospital environment. These olfactory triggers can transport him back to those frightening moments with startling clarity. For instance, the scent of antiseptic or a specific type of medical equipment can instantly bring back the intense fear he felt during his treatment. When these memories resurface, they are not just recollections; John feels as though he is reliving the event in real-time. The intensity and vividness of these flashbacks exacerbate his negative emotions, making him feel overwhelmed with fear, anger, and guilt. This reliving of trauma has led to a profound loss of faith—not only in people but also in life itself. He struggles to trust others or find hope in the future. John's heightened state of alertness is deeply intertwined with these memories and his resulting negative appraisals. The constant hypervigilance reinforces his belief that the world is dangerous, making it difficult for him to let down his guard even in familiar settings. This fear has also led to a sense that his body itself is an enemy, constantly reacting as if he were still under threat. John's occupation and daily environment have been significantly impacted by these experiences. As a Database Administrator, the sterile and controlled environment of his previous workplace now seems suffocatingly similar to the hospital setting he endured. The antiseptic smells in particular trigger intrusive memories that disrupt his concentration and peace of mind. He has become increasingly isolated, avoiding social interactions and even familiar environments due to these triggers. The cumulative effect of these experiences has left John feeling profoundly alone and disillusioned with life. His loss of faith extends beyond just people; he now views the world as a place filled with constant danger and uncertainty. This negative outlook has eroded his sense of safety, making it difficult for him to engage in daily activities without being overwhelmed by anxiety. What finally prompted John to seek help was a particularly intense flashback triggered by an unexpected scent at a family gathering. The overwhelming fear and guilt he experienced during this episode made him realize that his quality of life had drastically diminished. He is most afraid of continuing to live in this constant state of heightened alertness, where the past continues to intrude upon his present. John hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy and trust in the world around him. He wants to be able to feel safe again and move forward without being constantly haunted by memories that make him believe he is still under threat. The realization that these experiences have taken over his life has motivated him to seek support and understanding, hoping for a chance at reclaiming his peace of mind and faith in the world.
